hints: Focus on what each measurement tells you, each product contains only one element that came from thyroxine, so convert it back to moles of C, N and I.
Work out moles of $\text{AgI}$, $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{N}_2$ first, remembering $n = m/M_r$ for solids and $n = V/24000$ for gases in $\text{cm}^3$ at room conditions.
Use the moles of nitrogen atoms to find the moles of thyroxine in 0.500 g, then divide moles of C and I by that to get atoms per molecule and match to a formula.
walkthrough:
**Find moles of iodine from silver iodide**

All the iodine in thyroxine ends up as $\text{AgI}$. So moles of I atoms equals moles of $\text{AgI}$.

$$M_r(\text{AgI}) = 107.9 + 126.9 = 234.8$$
$$n(\text{AgI}) = \frac{0.604}{234.8} = 0.00257 \text{ mol}$$
So $n(\text{I}) = 0.00257$ mol in 0.500 g thyroxine.

**Find moles of carbon and nitrogen from combustion**

Complete combustion converts all C to $\text{CO}_2$ and all N to $\text{N}_2$. Use the room molar volume, $24000 \text{ cm}^3 \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

$$n(\text{CO}_2) = \frac{232}{24000} = 0.00967 \text{ mol} = n(\text{C})$$
$$n(\text{N}_2) = \frac{7.72}{24000} = 0.000322 \text{ mol}$$
Remember each $\text{N}_2$ has two N atoms:
$$n(\text{N}) = 2 \times 0.000322 = 0.000644 \text{ mol}$$

**Link to moles of thyroxine and atoms per molecule**

All the options contain one N per formula unit except C and D which are doubled. Let $n(\text{thyroxine})$ be moles in 0.500 g.

If there is 1 N per molecule, then $n(\text{thyroxine}) = n(\text{N}) = 0.000644$ mol.

Now divide:
$$\text{C per molecule} = \frac{0.00967}{0.000644} \approx 15.0$$
$$\text{I per molecule} = \frac{0.00257}{0.000644} \approx 4.0$$
This gives $\text{C}_{15}$ ... $\text{N}_{1}$ ... $\text{I}_{4}$, which fits $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_{4}\text{I}_{4}$ with $M_r = 776.6$. Check: $0.500/776.6 = 0.000644$ mol, perfect match.

options.A: Correct. 0.500 g is 0.000644 mol of $M_r$ 776.6. This predicts $15 \times 0.000644 = 0.00966$ mol $\text{CO}_2$ (232 $\text{cm}^3$), $0.5 \times 0.000644 = 0.000322$ mol $\text{N}_2$ (7.73 $\text{cm}^3$) and $4 \times 0.000644 = 0.00258$ mol $\text{AgI}$ (0.605 g). All three agree with experiment.
options.B: Incorrect. This has 8 iodines with a much larger $M_r$. 0.500 g would be only 0.000391 mol, giving $8 \times 0.000391 = 0.00313$ mol $\text{AgI}$ or about 0.734 g, far higher than 0.604 g. Students choosing this may have miscounted iodine or ignored the mass check.
options.C: Incorrect. Doubling carbon to $\text{C}_{30}$ predicts far too much $\text{CO}_2$. 0.500 g of $M_r$ 1002.6 is 0.000499 mol, giving $30 \times 0.000499 = 0.0150$ mol $\text{CO}_2$ or about 359 $\text{cm}^3$, not 232 $\text{cm}^3$. It also predicts only 2 iodines per 30 carbons, giving too little $\text{AgI}$.
options.D: Incorrect. Although the C:I:N ratio looks similar when halved, the large $M_r$ of 1506.2 fails the absolute amounts. 0.500 g is only 0.000332 mol, giving $30 \times 0.000332 = 0.00996$ mol C (close) but $8 \times 0.000332 = 0.00266$ mol I and $1 \times 0.000332$ mol N, which is only half the observed nitrogen. The trap is to look at ratios only and forget to check moles via $M_r$.
